text.title: Tree Testing Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for tree testing: stripping the tree to labels and hierarchy, reporting success and directness as separate metrics, wording tasks without echoing labels, fixing accepted destinations before launch, recruiting a sample large enough to report rates, and randomising a capped task set.

rule.statement: The `tree` under test MUST contain labels and parent-child structure only: no search box, no icons, no styling, no homepage promos, no cross-links or shortcut paths. Participants navigate by expanding levels and pick one destination.

rationale.source: Tree testing / reverse card sorting method (Spencer, Card Sorting: Designing Usable Categories, 2009; Optimal Workshop Treejack methodology)

rule.rationale: The method isolates one variable — whether the labels and grouping communicate where things live. Leave search in and participants route around bad structure, producing a healthy score for a tree that nobody could navigate; add visuals and you are measuring the visual design's ability to compensate.

rule.statement: `results` MUST report success (finished at an accepted destination) and directness (reached it without backing up a level) as separate per-task numbers. A task with high success and low directness MUST be listed in `problem_areas` as a label ambiguity, not counted as a pass.

rationale.source: Treejack / tree-testing metric definitions; first-click research (Bailey & Wolfson) on first click predicting task outcome

rule.rationale: Participants recover from a wrong branch by backing out, so success alone hides which branch attracted them first. The wrong first branch is what predicts real-world failure — a live user with no facilitator watching does not persist through three levels of backtracking, they use search or leave.

rule.statement: Scenario prompts MUST be written in user vocabulary and MUST NOT contain any word that appears in the target label or in any of its ancestor labels. Check each task against its path before launch; where the only natural phrasing reuses the label, rewrite the scenario as a situation rather than a request.
rule.rationale: A shared word turns the exercise into string matching down the tree, and the task passes regardless of whether the label conveys its concept. The result is a validated IA that fails as soon as real users arrive with their own words for the same thing.

rule.statement: Every task MUST declare its accepted destination or destinations before data collection, stored in the artefact. Destinations MUST NOT be added after seeing where participants went. If two destinations are genuinely both correct, that MUST be recorded as a duplicate-content finding in `problem_areas`.

rationale.source: Internal — pre-registration discipline applied to IA testing

rule.rationale: Post-hoc acceptance makes the success rate unfalsifiable: the analyst can move it to any value by widening the answer key, and widening always happens in the direction of the tree they built. Freezing the key first converts a defensible-sounding number into an actual measurement.

rule.statement: Tree testing is quantitative: target on the order of 50 participants per tree variant, with about 30 as the floor. Below that floor the artefact MUST report counts and observed paths rather than percentages, and MUST NOT claim that one tree variant beat another.

rationale.source: Optimal Workshop / NN/g sample-size guidance for quantitative IA testing

rule.rationale: Per-task success is a proportion, and at n=10 its confidence interval spans tens of percentage points — wider than any realistic difference between two candidate trees. Reporting "68% success" from ten people gives a decimal-precision veneer to a number that could as easily be 40 or 90.

rule.statement: No more than about 10 tasks per participant, and task order MUST be randomised per participant. The artefact MUST state both. Tasks whose target sits on a path already traversed by an earlier task MUST be spread apart or flagged.

rationale.source: Tree-testing administration guidance (Optimal Workshop); within-subject learning effects

rule.rationale: Participants learn the tree while being tested on it, so a fixed order systematically inflates the later tasks and the report concludes the deep branches are fine. Randomising spreads the learning effect evenly across tasks instead of concentrating it at the end of the list.

rule.statement: Skip when (a) no candidate hierarchy exists yet — run an open card sort first and tree-test the result; (b) the product's primary access path is search, a feed or deep links rather than navigation; (c) the question is about page content, wording of body copy or visual design — that is usability testing; (d) only one or two label candidates need checking and no quantitative sample is reachable — run a first-click test or a label-comprehension study instead.

rationale.source: Methodology preconditions for IA evaluation (card sorting to tree testing sequence)

rule.rationale: Tree testing evaluates a structure; it cannot generate one. Run without a candidate tree it produces failure data with no alternative to compare against, and the team rewrites labels reactively one failed task at a time.
